title: Inside the personal-care deferral: outliers, late and impossible claims
question: What did the federal agency find when it tested California’s personal-care claims, and how did it reach the amounts it withheld?
finding: The personal-care item is $1.13 billion for the quarter ended 2025-12-31; $646.4 million for the quarter ended 2026-03-31; $1.09 billion for the quarter ended 2026-06-30. Each time part is an estimate from growth faster than in other states, and part comes from tests on the State’s claims. Quarter ended 2025-12-31: $698.9 million statistical outliers; $13.2 million paid more than a year after the service. Quarter ended 2026-03-31: $237.5 million statistical outliers; $19.2 million paid more than a year after the service; $25.1 million one provider billing for four or more people; $3.8 million billed while the person was in hospital; $503,817 service after eligibility ended; $1,638 more than 283 hours in a month. Quarter ended 2026-06-30: $209.1 million statistical outliers; $16.0 million paid more than a year after the service; $19.9 million one provider billing for four or more people; $322,181 service dated after the person’s death; $591,611 billed by a provider after termination or exclusion; $3.8 million for people flagged as without satisfactory immigration status; $233,736 billed while the person was in hospital; $326,820 service after eligibility ended; $4,902 more than 283 hours in a month. In October it also asked about $305.6 million of employer payroll taxes and sick leave, and $209.0 million of “beneficiary services” it could not get explained.
how: The personal-care paragraph of each letter was split into its components and the dollar amounts it gives for each test, as worded in the letter. Amounts are federal share.
limits: These are the federal agency’s screening results while it reviews a sample; a statistical outlier is a claim to check, not a false one. The letters do not say which counties or providers the claims come from. In-Home Supportive Services in San Francisco is run by the county, but nothing in these letters places any amount in San Francisco. In the July letter one test reads “after the beneficiaries date of services”; the October letter has the same test as “after the beneficiaries date of death”, which suggests a typing error in the July letter.
